steps.title: Making charts readable with labels
steps.lede: A chart without labels is just shapes. Three Axes methods and one legend call fix that.

blocks.text: Titles, axis labels, and legends are the text that tells a reader what a plot shows. Matplotlib gives two parallel ways to add them: the Axes object interface and the pyplot interface. On an Axes object, ax.set_xlabel('Day'), ax.set_ylabel('Average delivery time (minutes)'), and ax.set_title('Average delivery time by day') label the Lagos trend line.

When you plot multiple series on the same Axes, a legend shows which line is which. Pass label='Lagos' to ax.plot(), then call ax.legend(). Once a second city's line is added to the same Axes, the legend identifies each series by its label.

before.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
days = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
lagos_avg = [21, 23, 19, 25, 20]
ax.plot(days, lagos_avg)
plt.show()
# No title, no axis labels, no legend

annotations.text: Plot draws, but the reader has no context

after.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
days = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
lagos_avg = [21, 23, 19, 25, 20]
ax.plot(days, lagos_avg, label='Lagos')
ax.set_xlabel('Day')
ax.set_ylabel('Average delivery time (minutes)')
ax.set_title('Average delivery time by day')
ax.legend()
plt.show()

annotations.text: label= kwarg names this series for the legend
set_xlabel, set_ylabel, set_title add axis labels and title

blocks.change_summary: Adding set_xlabel, set_ylabel, set_title, and legend turns an unlabeled plot into a self-explanatory chart.

blocks.text: In the pyplot interface, plt.xlabel(), plt.ylabel(), and plt.title() set the same label and title elements on the current Axes—the pyplot equivalents of ax.set_xlabel(), ax.set_ylabel(), and ax.set_title().

public.prompt: You have an Axes object called `ax`. Which three method calls correctly add a title, an x-axis label, and a y-axis label to that Axes?

opt_correct.message: Correct. `ax.set_xlabel()`, `ax.set_ylabel()`, and `ax.set_title()` are the three Axes object methods for labeling.

opt_plt.message: Those are the pyplot interface functions (`plt.xlabel()`, etc.), not the Axes object methods. The Axes object uses `ax.set_xlabel()`, `ax.set_ylabel()`, and `ax.set_title()`.

opt_fig.message: The Figure object (`fig`) does not have `set_xlabel()`, `set_ylabel()`, or `set_title()` methods. Labeling calls go on the Axes object (`ax`), not the Figure.

opt_mixed.message: The Axes methods are `ax.set_xlabel()`, `ax.set_ylabel()`, and `ax.set_title()` — note the `set_` prefix. `ax.xlabel()` and `ax.ylabel()` are not valid method names.

correct.message: Right. The Axes object's labeling methods all start with `set_`: `ax.set_xlabel()`, `ax.set_ylabel()`, and `ax.set_title()`.

incorrect.message: The Axes object uses `ax.set_xlabel('...')`, `ax.set_ylabel('...')`, and `ax.set_title('...')` — each takes a string argument.

hints: All three Axes labeling methods start with `set_`.
The methods belong to the `ax` object, not to `fig` or `plt`.

public.prompt: You are using the pyplot interface (no explicit `ax` variable). Which call sets the title of the current Axes?

opt_plt_title.message: Correct. In the pyplot interface, `plt.title()` sets the title of the current Axes — the pyplot equivalent of `ax.set_title()`.

opt_ax_title.message: `ax.set_title()` is the Axes object method, not the pyplot interface function. When using the pyplot interface without an explicit `ax`, use `plt.title()`.

opt_fig_title.message: The Figure object does not have a `set_title()` method for the Axes title. In the pyplot interface, use `plt.title()` to set the current Axes title.

opt_plt_set.message: `plt.set_title()` is not a valid pyplot function. The correct pyplot function is `plt.title()` (no `set_` prefix).

correct.message: Correct. `plt.title()`, `plt.xlabel()`, and `plt.ylabel()` are the pyplot interface equivalents of the Axes `set_` methods.

incorrect.message: In the pyplot interface, the labeling functions are `plt.title()`, `plt.xlabel()`, and `plt.ylabel()` — they operate on the current Axes without needing an explicit `ax` variable.

hints: The pyplot interface functions mirror the Axes methods but are called on `plt` directly.
Unlike the Axes methods, the pyplot functions do not have a `set_` prefix — it's `plt.title()`, not `plt.set_title()`.

steps.title: Practice
steps.lede: Add a title, axis labels, and a legend to an unlabeled plot.

public.prompt:
Two series are already plotted on `ax`: Lagos daily averages and Abuja daily averages for days 1–5.

Complete the code to:
1. Set the Axes title to `'Average Delivery Time by Day'`
2. Set the x-axis label to `'Day'`
3. Set the y-axis label to `'Average delivery time (minutes)'`
4. Add a legend that shows two entries — one labelled `'Lagos'` and one labelled `'Abuja'`

Use `ax.set_title()`, `ax.set_xlabel()`, `ax.set_ylabel()`, and `ax.legend()`. Pass `label='Lagos'` and `label='Abuja'` to the two `ax.plot()` calls already in the starter.

files.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

# Data (these values will be changed by the grader to test your code)
day_1 = 1
days = [day_1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
lagos_1 = 21
lagos_avg = [lagos_1, 23, 19, 25, 20]
abuja_1 = 24
abuja_avg = [abuja_1, 26, 22, 28, 25]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, lagos_avg)  # add label='Lagos' here
ax.plot(days, abuja_avg)  # add label='Abuja' here

# Add title, axis labels, and legend below

solution_files.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

# Data (these values will be changed by the grader to test your code)
day_1 = 1
days = [day_1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
lagos_1 = 21
lagos_avg = [lagos_1, 23, 19, 25, 20]
abuja_1 = 24
abuja_avg = [abuja_1, 26, 22, 28, 25]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, lagos_avg, label='Lagos')
ax.plot(days, abuja_avg, label='Abuja')

ax.set_title('Average Delivery Time by Day')
ax.set_xlabel('Day')
ax.set_ylabel('Average delivery time (minutes)')
ax.legend()

steps.eyebrow: Matching chart type to the analytical question
steps.title: Choosing the right chart for your question
steps.lede: Five chart types, five different questions. The chart you pick changes what the reader sees.

blocks.text: With five chart types available, the question during exploration is which one actually answers the question you're asking of the data. Picking a chart type comes down to naming what you're asking: a category comparison, a single variable's spread, a trend over time, a relationship between two variables, or a spread comparison across several groups.

A bar chart compares values across categories—average delivery time per city. plt.hist() bins a numeric variable and draws its distribution—how delivery times are spread out. Line graphs show how a value changes over time—average delivery time across days of the week. A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numeric variables—whether distance and delivery time move together. Boxplots compare the distributions of multiple datasets side by side—the full spread of delivery times across several cities at once.

blocks.left_label: Bar chart — Which city is slowest?
blocks.right_label: Line chart — How does time change by day?

left.title: Average Delivery Time by City
left.alt_text: Bar chart of average delivery time per city (Lagos, Abuja, Kano). Each bar represents one city's mean delivery time in minutes.

right.title: Lagos Delivery Time — Days 1–5
right.alt_text: Line chart of Lagos average delivery times across 5 days: 21, 23, 19, 25, 20 minutes. The connected line shows day-to-day variation.

blocks.takeaway: The same delivery data can be visualized multiple ways. Pick the chart type that answers your specific question.

segments.label: When a boxplot's distribution purpose doesn't fit the data at hand
segments.summary: The presenter sketches a boxplot as a candidate for a dataset where most groups have only one observation per day. Because a boxplot needs enough values per group to form a box, the sketch collapses to single points for nearly every day — making the chart unreadable. The presenter also notes that boxplots carry a steeper learning curve for unfamiliar audiences, though domain experts such as researchers may handle them fine. The conclusion is that sketching the option was worthwhile precisely to rule it out.

segments.label: Building a histogram with plt.hist() to reveal an age-group distribution
segments.summary: Starting from a list of ages, the presenter defines a set of numeric bins (0, 10, 20, … 130) and calls plt.hist() with the data list, the bins argument, histtype='bar', and rwidth=0.8. Running the code produces a bar-per-bin chart; the presenter reads the result aloud — the largest group falls between 40 and 50, no one appears in the 10–20 range — showing how the histogram surfaces the shape of the distribution rather than individual counts per label.

steps.title: Check your understanding

public.prompt: A QuickDeliver analyst wants to answer: 'What is the shape of the distribution of delivery times — are most deliveries fast, or is the spread wide?' Which chart type is best?

opt_hist.message: Correct. `plt.hist()` bins a numeric variable, counts values per bin, and draws the distribution as bars — exactly what you need to see the shape of delivery times.

opt_bar.message: A bar chart compares a numeric value across discrete categories (e.g., average delivery time per city). It does not show the distribution shape of a single numeric variable.

opt_line.message: A line graph shows how a value changes over time. It does not reveal the distribution shape of a numeric variable like delivery times.

opt_scatter.message: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables. To see the distribution of a single variable, use a histogram.

correct.message: Right. A histogram bins the data and shows how many values fall in each range — perfect for seeing the distribution shape.

incorrect.message: To see how a numeric variable is distributed (its shape, spread, and concentration), use a histogram (`plt.hist()`). Each bar represents a count of values in a bin.

hints: The question asks about the 'shape of the distribution' of a single numeric variable.
Think about which chart type bins a numeric variable and counts values per bin.

steps.eyebrow: Matching chart type to the analytical question
steps.title: Check your understanding

public.prompt: An analyst wants to compare the full spread of delivery times (median, quartiles, and outliers) across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano side by side. Which chart type is best?

opt_box.message: Correct. Box plots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side — showing median, quartiles, and outliers per group.

opt_line.message: A line graph shows how a value changes over time. It does not show the spread (quartiles, outliers) of a distribution across groups.

opt_hist.message: A histogram shows the distribution of a single numeric variable. To compare distributions across multiple groups side by side, a box plot is more compact and direct.

opt_bar.message: A bar chart compares a single aggregate value (like the mean) per category. It does not show the full spread — quartiles, median, and outliers — that a box plot provides.

correct.message: Exactly. A box plot condenses each group's distribution into a single visual — median, IQR, whiskers, and outliers — making side-by-side comparison easy.

incorrect.message: When you need to compare the full spread (median, quartiles, outliers) across multiple groups, a box plot is the right choice. It shows all of that in a compact form per group.

hints: The question asks for 'full spread' across multiple groups — which chart type shows quartiles and outliers per group?
A line graph tracks change over time; a box plot compares distributions across groups.

blocks.text: ax.set_xlabel(), ax.set_ylabel(), and ax.set_title() add axis labels and a title to an Axes object. Passing label= to a plot call and then calling ax.legend() adds a legend. In the pyplot interface, plt.xlabel(), plt.ylabel(), and plt.title() do the same.

Chart type follows the question: bar for category comparison, histogram for distribution, line for trends over time, scatter for relationships between two numeric variables, and boxplot for spread comparison across groups.

steps.title: Let's review
steps.lede: Here's another way to think about Axes labeling methods.

blocks.text: Think of the three set_* methods as captions for each part of the chart. ax.set_xlabel('Day') labels the x-axis. ax.set_ylabel('Average delivery time (minutes)') labels the y-axis. ax.set_title('Average delivery time by day') gives the whole chart a headline. Without these, the reader has to guess what the numbers mean.

blocks.text: Ask yourself: What question am I answering? Comparing cities (which is fastest?) → bar chart. Showing how delivery times are spread out → histogram.
